s1.name: Uncertainty & risk
s1.blurb: How to describe a risky choice with numbers (expected value, variance) and why attitudes to risk show up in the **shape** of a utility curve.
s1.metaphor: Think of a **coin flip for your rent money**. The expected value is the average result if you could flip forever. A risk-averse person feels the loss much more than the win, so a bet that's fair *on average* still feels like a bad deal.

topics.title: Objective and subjective probability
topics.html:
Objective (frequency) probability comes from how often something happened in many repetitions: a factory's defect rate, a coin landing heads.

Subjective probability is a personal judgment, used for events that happen only once: who wins this election, whether a new product will succeed. Different people can hold different subjective probabilities for the same event.

topics.title: Expected value: a probability-weighted average
topics.html:
$$E(X) = \Pr_1 X_1 + \Pr_2 X_2 + \dots + \Pr_n X_n$$

Multiply each outcome by its probability and add up. More likely outcomes pull the average towards themselves.

Seminar quiz, Scenario 1
Randy: 0.2 × \$15,000 + 0.8 × \$20,000 = **\$19,000**. Samantha: 0.25 × \$12,000 + 0.75 × \$20,000 = **\$18,000**. Randy expects to pay more.
Seminar quiz, Scenario 2
Turn "8 good years out of 10" into a probability of 0.8. Firm A: 0.8 × 8 + 0.2 × 6 = **7.6**; B: 6.4; C: 0.1 × 30 + 0.9 × 1 = 3.9. A wins.
Exam trap
A big number that rarely happens (firm C's \$30 million in 1 year out of 10) barely moves the expected value. Always weight by probability.

topics.title: Measuring risk: variance and standard deviation
topics.html:
$$\sigma^2 = \Pr_1 [X_1 - E(X)]^2 + \Pr_2 [X_2 - E(X)]^2 + \dots \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}$$

Expected value tells you the centre; variance and standard deviation tell you the spread, i.e. how far the outcomes typically land from the centre. Spread is what risk means.

Firm (Scenario 2)Expected revenueStandard deviation
A7.60.8
C3.98.7

Firm C is both worse on average and far riskier.

Remember
Expected value is not a measure of risk. Variance and standard deviation are.

topics.title: Risk premium: why people pay to avoid risk
topics.html:
The certainty equivalent is the sure amount that gives the same utility as the gamble. For a risk-averse person it is less than the expected value. The gap is the risk premium: what they would pay to get rid of the risk.

That's why risk-averse people buy insurance, and why they refuse gambles that are even slightly better than fair: the uncertainty costs them more utility than the small expected gain adds.

s2.name: Market interventions & welfare
s2.blurb: Consumer and producer surplus, why a free competitive market is efficient, and what price controls, quotas, taxes and externalities do to it.
s2.metaphor: Picture the market as a **meeting place where every trade worth more to the buyer than it costs the seller goes ahead**. Surplus is the value created by all those trades. Price controls, quotas and taxes block some of them, and the trades that never happen are the **deadweight loss**.

topics.title: Consumer and producer surplus
topics.html:
Consumer surplus = what a buyer would be willing to pay − what they actually pay. Producer surplus = what the seller receives − the least they'd accept (minus any extra costs the seller has to cover).

Seminar quiz: Jhon's violin
He'd accept anything above \$15,500, gets \$22,400, but must pay \$700 delivery: \$22,400 − \$15,500 − \$700 = **\$6,200**.

topics.title: Why the competitive equilibrium is efficient
topics.html:
At the competitive equilibrium the marginal benefit to buyers equals the marginal cost to sellers, so every trade worth making happens and no other. Total surplus is as large as it can be (when there are no externalities).

Pareto efficient
At that point you can't make anyone better off without making someone else worse off.

topics.title: Price ceilings and price floors
topics.html:
• A ceiling below equilibrium is binding. Quantity supplied falls, causing a shortage, and fewer units are traded.
  • A floor above equilibrium is binding. Quantity demanded falls, causing excess supply, and fewer units are traded.

Either way, trade happens on the short side of the market, and the lost trades are deadweight loss.

Try itMove the ceiling or floor
Exam trap
Consumers can lose from a price ceiling when demand is inelastic: the units that disappear were worth a lot to them. Try "Inelastic demand" in the diagram above.

topics.title: Price supports, quotas and tariffs
topics.html:
To hold a price up, a government can set a minimum price, buy up the surplus (a price support), or keep out cheaper imports with a tariff.

Production limits (taxi licences, crop acreage) shift supply left. With demand unchanged, the price rises and quantity falls.

topics.title: Reading surplus areas when supply shifts
topics.html:
Producer surplus is the area between the price and the supply curve. When supply falls from $S_1$ to $S_2$:

  • Gain b: the higher price on units still sold.
  • Lose e: those units now cost more to produce.
  • Lose f: surplus on units no longer sold.

So the change in producer surplus = b − f − e. Consumers lose b and c. Areas c and f plus the cost increase are what society loses.

topics.title: Who really pays a tax
topics.html:
Whoever is less able to walk away pays more of a tax, whatever the law says about who writes the cheque.

Formula: the share passed on to consumers is $\dfrac{E_s}{E_s - E_d}$.

topics.title: Externalities
topics.html: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on third parties without being priced: pollution (negative), vaccinations or education (positive). Private and social costs or benefits diverge, so the market produces too much of a negative-externality good, too little of a positive one, and is inefficient.

s3.name: Price discrimination
s3.blurb: How a firm with market power captures consumer surplus by charging different prices: to each customer (1st degree), by quantity (2nd) or by group (3rd).
s3.metaphor: A single price is like **selling concert tickets at one price to everyone**: fans who'd pay double keep the difference, and students who'd pay a little less stay home. Price discrimination is the art of charging each person or group closer to what they're **willing to pay**.

topics.title: Why one price leaves money on the table
topics.html:
At a single price $P^*$, buyers in range A pay less than they'd be willing to (they keep consumer surplus), and buyers in range B, who value the good above marginal cost, don't buy at all. To capture both, charge more to those willing to pay more and less to those willing to pay less.

The single-price trade-off
Cutting the price wins new buyers, but every existing customer pays less too. Price discrimination gets the new sales without giving everyone the discount.

topics.title: First-degree: everyone pays their reservation price
topics.html:
• Each customer pays their reservation price (maximum willingness to pay).
  • Consumer surplus = 0: the firm captures all of it.
  • Selling one more unit doesn't lower the price on the others, so MR = the demand curve.
  • Output expands to where demand meets MC, so there's no deadweight loss.
Try itSingle price vs perfect vs block pricing

Compared with a single price (profit = A), perfect discrimination adds the old consumer surplus B plus the old deadweight loss C + D.

topics.title: Second-degree: prices by quantity
topics.html: Different prices for different quantities or blocks: bulk discounts, block pricing of electricity. Customers sort themselves by how much they buy, so the firm doesn't need to know each person's reservation price.

topics.title: Third-degree: different prices for different groups
topics.html:
Split customers into groups (children and adults, students, regions) and charge each group a different price.

$$MR_1 = MR_2 = MC, \qquad MR = P\left(1 + \frac{1}{E}\right)$$

If one group's last unit earned more MR, you'd shift sales towards it. So in the end, MR is equal across groups, and equal to MC.

Who pays more?
The group with the less elastic demand (less price-sensitive) pays the higher price.
Try itThe coupon question, step by step

s4.name: Monopolistic competition & oligopoly
s4.blurb: Markets with many firms selling slightly different products, and markets dominated by a few firms who watch each other (Cournot).
s4.metaphor: Monopolistic competition is **a street full of cafés**: each one has a little monopoly over people who love its coffee, but if cafés make good money, new ones open next door until the extra profit is gone.

topics.title: What monopolistic competition looks like
topics.html:
• Many firms, differentiated products, free entry and exit.
  • Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it is not a price taker.
  • It produces where MR = MC, which leaves P > MC, always.

topics.title: Short run to long run: entry wipes out profit
topics.html:
Reading the price: find Q where MR = MC, then go up to the demand curve. In this figure that's \$3, while ATC is \$2, so the firm makes a profit.

Try itLet new firms enter

Profit attracts entrants. Each incumbent's demand and MR shift left (inward), and its price and quantity fall, until demand just touches ATC: P = ATC, zero economic profit. Price is still above MC, and output is below the minimum of ATC: excess capacity.

Exam trap
\$1 is where MR meets MC, not the price. The price is always read from the demand curve.

topics.title: Oligopoly: a few firms watching each other
topics.html:
The one essential feature: a few firms produce most of the output. Products can be identical or differentiated. Barriers to entry (economies of scale, patents, reputation) keep it that way.

Strategic interdependence
One firm's choices noticeably affect the others, so each must think about how its rivals will react. That's what monopolistic competition doesn't have.

topics.title: Cournot: competing on quantities
topics.html:
Each firm picks its output taking the other's output as given. A reaction curve shows a firm's best output for each output of its rival. The Cournot equilibrium is where the reaction curves cross: each firm is doing its best given the other, so neither wants to change alone (a Nash equilibrium).

Try itReaction curves and four market outcomes

s5.name: Oligopoly strategy & game theory
s5.blurb: What happens when the order of moves matters (Stackelberg), when firms compete on price (Bertrand), and why cartels are hard to hold together.
s5.metaphor: Oligopoly is **chess between a few firms**: every move (price, output) depends on what you expect the others to do, and moving first can be an advantage.

topics.title: The monopoly benchmark: MR = MC
topics.html:
With linear demand $p = a - bQ$, marginal revenue has twice the slope: $MR = a - 2bQ$. Set $MR = MC$ to get $Q$, then read the price off demand.

Seminar quiz
$p = 100 - 2Q$, $MC = 16$: $MR = 100 - 4Q = 16 \Rightarrow Q = 21$, and $p = 100 - 42 = 58$.
Exam trap
21 is the quantity, not the price. Always plug Q back into the demand curve.

topics.title: Stackelberg: the first-mover advantage
topics.html:
The leader chooses its output first, knowing how the follower will react. Because reaction curves slope down (more from the leader → lower price → less from the follower), the leader commits to a big output.

$$q_L = \frac{a - c}{2b}, \qquad q_F = \frac{a - c}{4b} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad q_L = 2q_F$$
Try itCompare cartel, Stackelberg, Cournot and Bertrand

topics.title: Bertrand: competing on price
topics.html: With identical products, buyers go to the cheaper firm, so a tiny price cut wins the whole market. Each firm keeps undercutting until price = marginal cost and profit is zero: the Bertrand paradox (two firms, yet the competitive outcome).

topics.title: Cartels and the prisoners' dilemma
topics.html:
Acting together as a cartel, firms can restrict output and earn monopoly profit. But each member can earn even more by cheating (producing more) while the others stick to the deal.

Try itThe cartel game
Escaping the dilemma
Firms escape by making collusion stick: an enforceable agreement, or a repeated game where cheating gets punished. Price-matching promises help hold collusion together.

topics.title: Why oligopolies exist and how they compete
topics.html:
• Economies of scale: only big producers reach low costs, so small entrants can't compete and only a few firms survive.
  • Strategic interdependence separates oligopoly from monopoly: both maximise profit, but an oligopolist must anticipate rivals.
  • Strategy covers technology, new markets and suppliers. What an oligopolist can't do is set its price ignoring its rivals.

questions.q: The expected value of a project is always the:
o: weighted average of the outcomes, with probabilities of the outcomes used as weights.
questions.x: Expected value = each outcome × its probability, added up: a **probability-weighted average**. The median and mode are other kinds of "middle", and the standard deviation measures spread (risk), not the average.

questions.q: Some individuals, when facing a lottery or other situation of uncertainty, prefer not to accept gambles that are better than fair (i.e., have a positive expected return), because of the negative utility they receive from uncertainty. What is the name for this behavior?
questions.x: Turning down a better-than-fair gamble because uncertainty itself feels bad is **risk aversion**. A risk-neutral person only looks at expected value, so they'd take it. Expected utility theory is the framework, not the behaviour.

questions.q: A person who is risk-loving by definition has a utility function with what shape?
questions.x: Risk-loving means each extra unit of wealth adds **more** utility than the last, so the curve gets steeper: **convex**. Concave means risk-averse; linear means risk-neutral.

questions.q: The risk-averse consumer has a ______ utility function, and its slope gets ______ as wealth is increased.
questions.x: Risk aversion = diminishing marginal utility. The curve is **concave**, and its slope (marginal utility) gets **flatter** as wealth rises. A slope never turns "vertical" because you got richer.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a generally accepted measure of the riskiness of an investment?
questions.x: Risk is about how far outcomes **spread** around the average, which is what variance and standard deviation measure. Expected value is the average itself, so it tells you nothing about risk.

questions.q: People often use probability statements to describe events that can only happen once. For example, a political consultant may offer their opinion about the probability that a particular candidate may win the next election. Probability statements like these are based on ____ probabilities.
questions.x: A one-off event can't be repeated to count how often it happens, so the probability is a personal judgment: **subjective** probability. Objective (frequency-based) probability comes from how often something happened over many repetitions.

questions.q: A person with a diminishing marginal utility of income:
questions.x: Diminishing marginal utility means losing \$100 hurts more than winning \$100 helps, so a fair gamble lowers expected utility and the person avoids it: **risk averse** (a concave utility curve).

questions.q: John's marginal utility of income function is given as $MU(I) = I$ (his income). From this you would say that he is:
questions.x: $MU(I) = I$ means marginal utility **rises** with income: each extra unit of income adds more utility than the last. That makes utility convex, so John is **risk-loving**. Constant MU would be risk-neutral; falling MU, risk-averse.

questions.q: A ______ set below the equilibrium price in a perfectly competitive market will result in a deadweight loss because it ______ the quantity supplied by producers.
questions.x: A ceiling set **below** equilibrium is binding. At the lower price producers supply less, so fewer units are traded. Trades worth more to buyers than they cost to produce never happen: that's the deadweight loss. A floor would be set *above* equilibrium.

questions.q: If the government plans to maintain a certain level of price for a specific good, what economic policy can it use to achieve this goal?
questions.x: All three hold the price up: a **minimum price** stops it falling below a level, a **price support** has the government buy up the surplus, and an **import tariff** keeps cheaper foreign supply out.

questions.q: In the context of market outcomes, an externality occurs when the actions of consumers or producers:
o: Impose uncompensated costs or benefits on third parties that are not reflected in the market price.
Lead to a divergence between private and social costs or benefits.
Result in market inefficiency because the price mechanism fails to capture all relevant costs or benefits.
questions.x: All three describe an externality: a cost or benefit lands on third parties without a price, so private and social costs (or benefits) differ, and the market outcome is inefficient.

questions.q: Which of the following CANNOT reduce the equilibrium quantity sold in a market?
questions.x: Each of them can cut the quantity sold. A quota caps it directly; a binding ceiling cuts the quantity **supplied**; a binding floor cuts the quantity **demanded**. Trade happens on the short side of the market, so the answer is "none of the above".

questions.q: A government limits the number of taxi licenses or the acreage used to grow wheat or corn. If consumer demand remains unchanged, what is the most likely effect of such a production limit?
o: The reduction in supply creates scarcity, causing the equilibrium price to rise.
The reduction in supply causes both the equilibrium price and quantity to rise.
The restriction has no effect on price because consumer demand has not changed.
The restriction causes the equilibrium price to fall because fewer units are available for consumers.
questions.x: Limiting licences or acreage shifts supply to the left. With demand unchanged, the price **rises** and the quantity falls. Quantity can't rise when supply is restricted (B).

questions.q: Consider the supply and demand diagram. If supply decreases from $S_1$ to $S_2$, which area represents the change in PRODUCER surplus?

After the shift producers **gain** *b* (the higher price on the units they still sell) but **lose** *e* (those units now cost more to make, since $S_2$ lies above $S_1$) and *f* (surplus on the units no longer sold). Change = **b − f − e**. Option B, a + b + c, is the original consumer surplus.

questions.q: Which one of these statements is true?
o: The more inelastic the demand, the greater the incidence of a tax on the producer.
The more elastic the demand, the smaller the incidence of a tax on the consumer.
If demand is perfectly inelastic, the whole incidence of the tax will be on the producer.
If demand is perfectly elastic, the whole incidence of the tax will be on the consumer.
questions.x: The less able buyers are to walk away (inelastic demand), the more of the tax they pay. So with **more elastic** demand, consumers bear **less** of it. The other three are back to front: perfectly inelastic demand puts the whole tax on consumers, and perfectly elastic demand puts it all on producers.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
o: At competitive equilibrium, market surplus is maximized.
At the competitive equilibrium, the marginal benefit to consumers equals the marginal cost to producers.
At the competitive equilibrium, social surplus is maximized if there are no externalities.
At the competitive equilibrium, it is possible to make at least one person better off without making anyone worse off.
questions.x: A competitive equilibrium is **Pareto efficient**: you **can't** make anyone better off without making someone worse off, so D is the false one. A–C are true: surplus is maximised where marginal benefit = marginal cost, as long as there are no externalities.

questions.q: Suppose a firm has market power and faces a downward sloping demand curve for its product, and its marginal cost curve is upward sloping. If the firm reduces its price, then:
o: producer surplus increases due to new buyers, but the producer surplus from existing customers declines due to the lower price.
the change in producer surplus is transferred to consumers.
the increase in consumer surplus is only due to the increase in quantity demanded.
the sum of producer and consumer surplus remains the same, but surplus value is transferred from the producer to consumers.
questions.x: A price cut wins **new** buyers (extra producer surplus on those units) but every **existing** customer now pays less too (lost producer surplus on them). That trade-off is why a single-price firm can't capture all the surplus, and why it would like to price-discriminate. D is wrong: total surplus changes too, because the deadweight loss shrinks.

questions.q: When a monopolist engages in perfect price discrimination,
o: the marginal revenue curve lies below the demand curve.
the demand curve and the marginal revenue curve are identical.
the marginal revenue curve becomes horizontal.
questions.x: With perfect price discrimination, selling one more unit doesn't lower the price on earlier units, so the extra revenue is just that unit's price: **MR = demand**. With a single price, MR lies below demand (option A).

questions.q: Which of the following is true regarding the long run for a firm in monopolistic competition?
questions.x: In the long run entry removes economic profit, so the demand curve just touches ATC and **P = ATC**. Price stays above MC (so B and D are wrong). MR = MC still holds, but at a level below ATC (so A is wrong).

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of oligopoly, but NOT of monopolistic competition?
o: Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
There is more than one firm in the industry.
The choices made by one firm have a significant effect on other firms.
questions.x: A–C are true of both. What sets oligopoly apart is **strategic interdependence**: with only a few firms, one firm's choices noticeably affect the others, so each must think about how its rivals will react.

questions.q: In the Cournot model, two firms simultaneously choose quantities, taking the quantity chosen by the other firm as given. At the Cournot equilibrium, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Each firm chooses the monopoly quantity because it assumes the other firm will produce zero.
Each firm chooses its profit-maximizing quantity given the quantity chosen by the other firm; therefore, neither firm can increase its profit by changing its quantity alone.
The market price must equal marginal cost because the two firms compete with each other.
The two firms maximize their joint profit by behaving as a single monopolist.
questions.x: Cournot equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium in quantities: each firm is on its **reaction curve**, giving its best response to the other's output, so neither gains by changing alone. Price stays above MC (C), and the firms don't reach the joint-monopoly profit (D).

questions.q: When a new firm enters a monopolistically competitive market or one firm introduces an improved product, the demand curve for each of the other firms shifts ______, reducing the ______ received by those incumbents.
questions.x: A new or better rival takes customers, so each incumbent's demand curve shifts **inward** (left). At every price it sells less, and it can only charge less, so **both price and quantity** fall.

questions.q: Which characteristic is essential for identifying an oligopolistic market, while the other characteristics may vary across oligopolies?
o: Firms must earn substantial economic profits in the long run.
A small number of firms account for most or all market production.
questions.x: The defining feature is that **a few firms produce most of the output**. Oligopoly products can be identical (steel) or differentiated (cars), and long-run profits vary, so A, B and D aren't essential.

questions.q: The relationship between a firm's profit maximizing output and the amount it thinks its competitor will produce refers to:
questions.x: A **reaction curve** shows a firm's profit-maximising output for each quantity it expects its rival to produce. Where two firms' reaction curves cross is the Cournot equilibrium.

questions.q: In a Stackelberg model, if firm 1 increases its output, the follower firm's best response will:
o: Increase, because the market price rises.
Decrease, because the market price falls.
Remain unchanged, because firm 2 ignores firm 1's output.
questions.x: More output from firm 1 pushes the market price **down**, so producing is less attractive for firm 2: its best response is to produce **less**. That's why reaction curves slope down.

questions.q: In a Stackelberg duopoly with zero marginal costs and inverse demand $p = a - bQ$, which of the following statements is TRUE?
o: The leader produces twice as much output as the follower at equilibrium.
The follower produces twice as much output as the leader at equilibrium.
Both firms produce the same quantity at equilibrium.
The follower produces zero output at equilibrium.
questions.x: The leader produces $\frac{a}{2b}$ and the follower $\frac{a}{4b}$, so the leader produces **twice** as much. Moving first lets the leader commit to a big output, and the follower has to accommodate it. Equal outputs (C) is Cournot.

questions.q: A key fundamental behavioral difference between monopoly and oligopoly is that:
o: Both monopoly and oligopoly firms generally aim to maximize profits, but oligopoly firms face strategic interdependence.
Deadweight loss due to market power.
A monopoly has no need to collude, but oligopoly firms often have incentives to collude to improve profits.
questions.x: Both maximise profit, but an oligopolist must take its rivals' reactions into account: **strategic interdependence**. A monopoly has no rivals to think about. B and C are features of market structure, not behaviour.

questions.q: If the inverse demand curve a monopoly faces is $p = 100 - 2Q$, and MC is constant at 16, then profit maximisation is achieved when the monopoly sets price equal to:
questions.x: With linear demand, MR has twice the slope: $MR = 100 - 4Q$. Set $MR = MC$: $100 - 4Q = 16 \Rightarrow Q = 21$. Then **read the price from demand**: $p = 100 - 2(21) = 58$. 21 is the quantity, not the price, and 16 is MC.

v.q: If the inverse demand curve a monopoly faces is $p = 66 - Q$, and MC is constant at 14, then profit maximisation is achieved when the monopoly sets price equal to:
v.x: $MR = 66 - 2Q$. Set $MR = MC$: $66 - 2Q = 14 \Rightarrow Q = 26$. Price comes from demand: $p = 66 - 1(26) = 40$.

v.x: $MR = 86 - 8Q$. Set $MR = MC$: $86 - 8Q = 6 \Rightarrow Q = 10$. Price comes from demand: $p = 86 - 4(10) = 46$.

questions.q: Collusion makes firms better off because if they act as a single entity (a cartel) they can reduce output and increase their prices and profits. But some cartels have failed, and others are unstable. Which of the following is a reason why cartels often break down?
o: Most cartels do not have a dominant strategy.
Each member of a cartel has an incentive to 'cheat' on the collusive agreement by producing more than its share when everyone else sticks with the collusive agreement.
When a cartel is profitable the amount of competition it faces increases.
Members of a cartel may resent having to share their profits equally.
questions.x: Each member can raise its **own** profit by producing more than its quota while the others hold back. Everyone has that incentive, so cartels tend to collapse. It's a prisoners' dilemma: try the cartel game on the Learn page.

questions.q: When two firms sell identical products and have the same constant cost, what price do they end up charging in the Bertrand competition?
o: A price above their cost to make profit
A price set through agreement to keep it high
questions.x: With identical products, buyers go to whoever is cheaper, so each firm undercuts the other until **price equals marginal cost**. This is the Bertrand paradox: just two firms, yet the competitive price.

questions.q: If one firm lowers its price just a little bit below the other firm's price in Bertrand competition, what happens?
o: The firm loses all its customers to the other firm
The firm gets all the customers
The other firm keeps its customers without changing price
questions.x: The products are identical, so every buyer goes to the cheaper firm: a tiny price cut wins the **whole** market. That incentive keeps pushing prices down to marginal cost.

questions.q: An oligopoly firm can escape the prisoners' dilemma by:
o: Ignoring the actions of other firms.
Advertising that it will match any price reduction made by competitors.
Colluding with other firms to agree on high prices and restrict output.
Increasing its production regardless of competitors' decisions.
questions.x: In the dilemma each firm's dominant strategy (cut price or raise output) leaves both worse off. Escaping it means **coordinating on the cooperative outcome**: colluding to keep prices high and output low, which can last when the game is repeated or the deal is enforced. That's the course's answer. Price-matching promises (B) look tempting because they help such collusion hold, but the escape itself is the collusion.

questions.q: Economies of scale can lead to an oligopoly market structure because:
o: A few firms can force rivals to produce at low levels of output.
A few firms can use high profits to keep out new entrants.
If larger firms have lower costs, new small entrants will not be able to produce at the low costs achieved by the big established firms.
If economies of scale are insignificant in production, only a few firms are able to produce at the low costs achieved by the big established firms.
questions.x: With big economies of scale, only large producers reach low average cost. A small newcomer can't match those costs, so the market supports only a **few** firms. D reverses the logic: if economies of scale were *insignificant*, many firms could compete.

questions.q: Which of the following is not part of an oligopolist's business strategy?
o: Independently setting a product's price without consideration of rivals' pricing policies.
Choosing what new technologies to adopt.
Selecting which new markets to enter.
Deciding on how to manage relations with suppliers.
questions.x: Ignoring rivals' prices is exactly what an oligopolist **can't** do: its profit depends on what rivals charge. Technology, new markets and supplier relations are all normal parts of its strategy.
